name: Azure Service Bus
oneLiner: Enterprise message broker with queues and topics for reliable decoupling.
whatItIs: Azure Service Bus is Azure's enterprise message broker — a fully-managed service for reliable, decoupled communication between applications and services. It offers queues (point-to-point) and topics/subscriptions (publish-subscribe fan-out), with enterprise messaging features: guaranteed ordering (sessions), exactly-once handling (dead-lettering, duplicate detection), transactions, and scheduled delivery. It's built for business-critical workloads where messages must not be lost or mishandled. In contrast to Event Hubs (high-throughput event streaming), Service Bus is about discrete commands/messages with rich delivery guarantees — the backbone for decoupling enterprise applications on Azure.

inPractice.narrative: An order system must reliably tell fulfilment, billing and notifications about each new order — without tight coupling. It publishes each order to a Service Bus topic; three subscriptions (fulfilment, billing, notifications) each receive their own copy and process independently, with dead-lettering catching failures and sessions preserving per-customer order. If a consumer is down, messages wait durably. Service Bus is the reliable broker decoupling enterprise services with strong delivery guarantees.

coreConcepts.detail: Queues are point-to-point (one consumer group competes for messages); topics with subscriptions fan out a copy of each message to multiple independent subscribers.
Message sessions guarantee FIFO ordering and stateful handling for related messages (e.g. all messages for one order/customer).
Failed or expired messages move to a dead-letter queue; duplicate detection discards repeats — enterprise reliability features beyond a basic queue.
Reliable delivery with peek-lock, plus transactions that group operations atomically — for workloads where correctness matters.
Standard (shared, pay-per-operation) and Premium (dedicated messaging units, predictable performance, VNet, larger messages) for enterprise scale/isolation.
Service Bus = discrete messages/commands with rich guarantees; Event Hubs = high-throughput event streaming. Different tools for different jobs.

whenToUse: Reliable, decoupled communication between enterprise applications.
Publish-subscribe fan-out to multiple independent consumers (topics).
Workloads needing ordering (sessions), dead-lettering or duplicate detection.
Transactional messaging where correctness is critical.
Command/message passing rather than high-volume event streaming.
whenNotToUse: High-throughput event/telemetry streaming — use Event Hubs.
Replayable event logs and stream analytics — Event Hubs/Kafka.
Simple, cheapest-possible queueing at massive scale where features aren't needed.
Real-time analytics pipelines — that's a streaming service.

keyFacts.label: Contrast
keyFacts.value: Discrete messages vs Event Hubs streaming.

keyFacts.label: Billing
keyFacts.value: Standard: per operation + base; Premium: per messaging unit.

pricingShape: Standard tier bills a base charge plus per-operation (messaging operations), suited to modest or variable workloads; Premium tier bills per messaging unit — dedicated capacity giving predictable performance, VNet isolation and larger messages — which is cost-effective and required at enterprise scale. So light workloads favour Standard's pay-per-use, while high-volume/critical workloads favour Premium's reserved capacity. The levers are choosing the tier by throughput and isolation needs, and being aware that the rich features (sessions, dead-lettering) are about reliability, not extra per-message fees.
gotchas: It's for discrete messages with guarantees, not high-throughput streaming — use Event Hubs for telemetry.
Standard vs Premium differ in performance, isolation and pricing model — pick deliberately for scale.
Sessions enable ordering but add handling complexity and can limit parallelism — use only when order matters.
Without configuring dead-lettering/TTL, failed messages can accumulate or block processing.
Consumers should be idempotent — at-least-once delivery plus retries can reprocess messages.
